items.stem: After massive resuscitation for a ruptured aortic aneurysm, a 74-year-old man has a tense, distended abdomen. Bladder pressure is 28 mm Hg, urine output is 10 mL per hour, peak airway pressures are rising, and he requires escalating vasopressors. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Large crystalloid boluses to improve renal perfusion and follow the creatinine over the next day
Furosemide infusion with continued current support
Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure
Repeat bladder pressure measurement in 12 hours
items.explanation: Sustained intra-abdominal pressure above 20 mm Hg with new organ dysfunction defines abdominal compartment syndrome, which causes oliguria, high airway pressures, and reduced venous return. Definitive treatment is decompressive laparotomy with a temporary closure. More fluid worsens edema and pressure. Diuretics are ineffective when the kidneys are under mechanical compression. Waiting for repeat measurement delays treatment while the patient deteriorates, and nonoperative measures are reserved for earlier stages.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids with regurgitation of undigested food and a 6-kg weight loss. Upper endoscopy shows a dilated esophagus with retained food and no mass. A barium swallow shows a tapered distal esophagus. Which test is best to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Esophageal pH monitoring
Repeat contrast study with water-soluble agent
Gastric emptying scintigraphy
High-resolution esophageal manometry
items.explanation: Dysphagia to solids and liquids with regurgitation and a tapered distal esophagus suggests achalasia, and endoscopy has excluded a mimicking tumor. Manometry is the confirmatory test, showing incomplete relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and absent peristalsis, and it also defines the subtype. Reflux monitoring evaluates acid exposure, not motility. Another contrast study adds little, and gastric emptying assesses gastroparesis. Heller myotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy, or dilation follows.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis has feculent peritonitis, a heart rate of 128, and blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg despite fluid resuscitation. Lactate is 5 mmol per liter. Which operation is most appropriate?
options: Sigmoid resection with end colostomy and closure of the rectal stump
Primary anastomosis without diversion, accepting the leak risk because the colon is unprepared
Laparoscopic lavage and drains alone
Percutaneous drainage and delayed elective resection
items.explanation: Generalized feculent peritonitis in an unstable patient is Hinchey IV, and the safest operation is the Hartmann procedure, resecting the diseased sigmoid with an end colostomy. Primary anastomosis in shock with gross contamination has an unacceptable leak risk. Lavage alone fails in feculent contamination. Percutaneous drainage suits a contained abscess, not diffuse peritonitis. Restoration of continuity is considered months later in suitable patients.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain and fever for 36 hours. Her temperature is 38.4 C, Murphy sign is positive, and the white blood cell count is 14,500. Ultrasound shows gallstones, a thickened wall, and pericholecystic fluid. The common duct is normal. She is otherwise healthy. What is the best management?
options: Antibiotics alone with elective surgery in three months
Antibiotics and laparoscopic cholecystectomy early in the admission
Immediate endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Percutaneous cholecystostomy as a routine first step
items.explanation: Acute calculous cholecystitis in a fit patient is treated with early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ideally within the first days of symptoms, which shortens stay and avoids recurrent attacks. Delayed surgery risks complications while waiting. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is for suspected common duct stones, which are absent here. Cholecystostomy is a bridge for patients too ill for operation, not the routine first choice.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 4 months ago for stable angina is scheduled for an elective ventral hernia repair. He takes aspirin and clopidogrel and has no current symptoms. He asks how to proceed. Which plan is best?
options: Proceed this week after stopping both aspirin and clopidogrel for 10 days and resuming them once the wound has healed
Proceed this week and start a bridging anticoagulant infusion instead
Cancel the repair permanently because any stent is an absolute contraindication
Postpone the elective repair until at least 6 months after stent placement and continue aspirin throughout
items.explanation: Premature interruption of dual antiplatelet therapy after a drug-eluting stent carries a high risk of stent thrombosis and myocardial infarction. Elective operations should wait until the recommended minimum course is complete, and aspirin is generally continued through surgery. Stopping both agents early exposes the stent, and bridging anticoagulation does not protect it. A stent is a reason to time surgery carefully, never a permanent bar to an operation.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a screening mammogram showing 1-cm clustered microcalcifications. Stereotactic core biopsy shows ductal carcinoma in situ, intermediate grade, estrogen receptor positive, with no invasive component. The lesion is unifocal. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Lumpectomy with negative margins and whole-breast radiation, with consideration of endocrine therapy
Lumpectomy alone with no further treatment
Modified radical mastectomy with full axillary dissection
Chemotherapy followed by observation, because the tumor has hormone receptors and a small size
items.explanation: Unifocal ductal carcinoma in situ can be treated with breast conservation plus whole-breast radiation, which cuts local recurrence, and endocrine therapy for hormone receptor positive disease reduces recurrence further. Omitting radiation is considered only in selected low-risk cases. Axillary dissection is unnecessary because in situ disease does not metastasize, and sentinel biopsy is only done if mastectomy is performed. Chemotherapy has no role in pure in situ disease.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with newly diagnosed small cell lung cancer has nausea and mild confusion. She is euvolemic. Serum sodium is 123 mEq per liter, serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is high, and urine sodium is above 40 mEq per liter. Thyroid and adrenal function are normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Rapid infusion of isotonic saline until sodium normalizes within hours
Free water restriction with treatment of the underlying tumor
Large-volume hypotonic fluid to dilute the concentrated urine
Bolus of 3 percent saline to correct sodium by 12 mEq per liter in a day
items.explanation: Euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urinary sodium is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, classically from small cell lung cancer. With mild symptoms, free water restriction is first-line, and the tumor is treated. Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatremia because the water is retained while sodium is excreted. Hypotonic fluids worsen it. Overly rapid correction, above about 8 to 10 mEq per liter in a day, risks osmotic demyelination.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has a 1.5-mm thick, nonulcerated melanoma on the calf, diagnosed by excisional biopsy. The groin has no palpable nodes and imaging shows no distant disease. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Excision with a 5-mm margin and no nodal evaluation, since the node basin is clinically negative
Wide excision with a 5-cm margin and elective groin dissection
Wide local excision with a 1-cm to 2-cm margin and sentinel lymph node biopsy
Systemic therapy as initial treatment
items.explanation: For a melanoma between 1 and 2 mm thick, the recommended margin is 1 to 2 cm, and sentinel node biopsy is advised because nodal status guides staging and adjuvant therapy. Narrow margins risk local recurrence. Margins beyond 2 cm confer no benefit, and routine elective lymph node dissection does not improve survival over sentinel biopsy. Systemic therapy has a role in advanced or node-positive disease, but not as first treatment here.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has three days of perineal pain, swelling, and fever. His heart rate is 124 and blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg. Examination shows scrotal skin that is dusky and crepitant, with pain out of proportion to the findings. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Intravenous antibiotics alone with repeat examination in 24 hours
Computed tomography first, with debridement only if gas tracks proximally
Incision and drainage of a single abscess cavity at the bedside
Resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and urgent radical surgical debridement
items.explanation: Crepitus, dusky skin, systemic toxicity, and pain out of proportion in a diabetic patient indicate necrotizing soft tissue infection of the perineum. Mortality rises with each hour of delay, so management is resuscitation, antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms, and prompt wide debridement, repeated as needed. Antibiotics alone cannot penetrate necrotic tissue. Imaging should never delay the operation, and simple drainage of an abscess is inadequate for a spreading fascial process.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man who smokes is found to have a 5.8-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound done for another reason. He is asymptomatic and has good functional status. Computed tomography shows suitable neck anatomy. What is the best recommendation?
options: Elective repair, with endovascular repair favored when anatomy is suitable
Surveillance ultrasound every year with repair deferred until the diameter reaches 6.5 cm
Beta-blocker therapy alone
Repair only if he develops back pain
items.explanation: Asymptomatic aneurysms of 5.5 cm or more in men carry a risk of rupture that exceeds elective repair risk, so repair is advised. Endovascular repair offers lower early morbidity when the neck and iliac anatomy are suitable, with lifelong imaging follow-up. Annual surveillance fits smaller aneurysms. Beta-blockers do not meaningfully prevent rupture. Waiting for pain risks rupture, which carries very high mortality, so symptoms signal urgent treatment.

items.stem: A 5-week-old boy has forceful nonbilious vomiting after every feeding and is hungry afterward. He has lost weight. Blood testing shows a sodium of 132, a potassium of 3.2, chloride of 88, and bicarbonate of 34 mEq per liter. After ultrasound confirms the diagnosis, what is the next step?
options: Immediate pyloromyotomy without correcting laboratory values
Fluid and electrolyte resuscitation before pyloromyotomy
A trial of acid-suppressing medication
Barium enema to exclude malrotation
items.explanation: Projectile nonbilious vomiting in an infant with a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It is a medical emergency, not a surgical one, and the alkalosis and dehydration should be corrected with isotonic fluid containing dextrose and potassium before operation to reduce anesthetic risk. Pyloromyotomy then cures the condition. Acid suppression does not treat the obstruction, and malrotation causes bilious vomiting.

items.stem: A randomized trial compares a new wound dressing with standard care. Surgical site infection occurred in 20 percent of the control group and 12 percent of the treatment group. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one infection?
options: Approximately 8 patients
Approximately 5 patients
Approximately 20 patients
Approximately 13 patients
items.explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 20 percent minus 12 percent, or 8 percent, which is 0.08. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal, 1 divided by 0.08, which equals 12.5, rounded up to 13. The figure 8 confuses the percentage points with the number. Five reflects an unrelated reciprocal of the control rate. Twenty uses the control group raw percentage. Relative risk reduction would be 40 percent but does not give the number needed to treat.

items.stem: A 31-year-old man is brought in 10 minutes after a stab wound to the left chest near the sternum. Blood pressure is 76/50 mm Hg, neck veins are distended, and heart sounds are muffled. The focused ultrasound shows fluid around the heart. Which is the best next step?
options: Percutaneous pericardiocentesis as definitive treatment
Computed tomography of the chest with contrast to define the extent of the cardiac injury first
Immediate operative exploration with pericardial decompression and cardiac repair
Large-volume crystalloid resuscitation and observation
items.explanation: Penetrating precordial injury with hypotension, distended neck veins, and pericardial fluid is cardiac tamponade requiring urgent operative decompression and repair of the cardiac wound. Pericardiocentesis is unreliable because blood clots and may only be a temporary bridge. Imaging delays the operation in an unstable patient. Fluids may temporarily raise preload but do not treat the cause. The pericardium is opened through sternotomy or thoracotomy in the operating room.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man who takes naproxen daily has sudden severe epigastric pain. He lies still with a rigid abdomen. Heart rate is 112 and blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg. An upright chest film shows free air under the diaphragm. After resuscitation, which operation is most appropriate?
options: Laparoscopic or open omental patch repair of the perforation with testing for Helicobacter pylori
Truncal vagotomy and antrectomy as the routine first choice
High-dose acid suppression alone with nasogastric decompression and serial abdominal examinations
Percutaneous drainage of the subphrenic collection
items.explanation: A rigid abdomen with free air indicates perforated peptic ulcer, and in most patients simple closure with an omental patch is sufficient, followed by acid suppression, stopping the anti-inflammatory drug, and treating Helicobacter pylori if found. Definitive acid-reducing operations are reserved for selected stable patients and carry more risk. Nonoperative therapy is only for a sealed perforation in a patient who is well. Drainage does not close the hole.

items.stem: An 82-year-old nursing home resident has abdominal distention and constipation. The film shows a massively dilated sigmoid loop forming a bent inner tube pointing toward the right upper quadrant. There is no peritonitis, and the sigmoidoscopy mucosa is viable. After detorsion, which plan is best?
options: Discharge with no further planned treatment
Elective sigmoid colectomy during the same admission to prevent recurrence
Repeat enemas weekly as definitive management because an elderly patient is unfit for any operation
Emergency subtotal colectomy
items.explanation: Sigmoid volvulus without ischemia is treated first with endoscopic detorsion, and because recurrence is common, often exceeding half of cases, resection of the redundant sigmoid is recommended during the same admission in fit patients. Emergency surgery is for gangrene or perforation. Discharge without resection invites recurrence. Enemas are not a definitive treatment. Subtotal colectomy is excessive for a localized sigmoid problem.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man has fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg and he is confused. Bilirubin is 6.8 mg per deciliter. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. After resuscitation and antibiotics, which step is most appropriate?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy tonight with no drainage
Antibiotics alone for 48 hours before reassessment
Urgent biliary decompression by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Elective magnetic resonance cholangiography next week
items.explanation: Fever, jaundice, pain, hypotension, and confusion constitute severe suppurative cholangitis, with obstructed infected bile under pressure. Antibiotics and resuscitation are paired with urgent decompression, preferably by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stone removal or stent placement. Percutaneous drainage is the alternative. Cholecystectomy does not drain the duct and is unsafe in shock. Waiting for antibiotics alone risks death, and delayed imaging is inappropriate for a critically ill patient.

items.stem: Thirty minutes into a general anesthetic with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a healthy 24-year-old man develops masseter rigidity, an end-tidal carbon dioxide that keeps climbing despite increased ventilation, a heart rate of 140, and a temperature of 38.9 C. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Give intravenous verapamil to control the tachycardia and continue the same anesthetic until the case is finished safely
Discontinue the volatile agent and give intravenous dantrolene while hyperventilating with 100 percent oxygen
Give intravenous neostigmine to reverse the neuromuscular blocker and continue
Apply surface cooling blankets and intravenous acetaminophen and observe the trend
items.explanation: This is malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile agents and succinylcholine. Treatment is to stop triggers, hyperventilate with oxygen, and give dantrolene, which blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium channel blockers combined with dantrolene risk hyperkalemia and are avoided. Neostigmine does not treat the disorder. Cooling and acetaminophen treat temperature only and delay the specific drug while metabolic acidosis and rhabdomyolysis progress.

items.stem: On the second day after total thyroidectomy for Graves disease, a 40-year-old woman reports tingling around the mouth and in her fingers. The Chvostek sign is positive. Serum calcium is 7.1 mg per deciliter with normal albumin. Which treatment should be given for her symptoms?
options: Intravenous furosemide to correct the electrolyte shift
Observation with oral magnesium only
Intravenous calcium gluconate followed by oral calcium and vitamin D
Parathyroid hormone antagonist therapy
items.explanation: Perioral numbness and a positive Chvostek sign after thyroidectomy indicate symptomatic hypocalcemia from devascularized or injured parathyroid glands, and a confirmed low calcium requires intravenous calcium gluconate, then oral calcium and active vitamin D until the glands recover. Observation risks tetany, laryngospasm, and seizure. Furosemide lowers calcium further. Magnesium is checked and replaced if low but is not sufficient alone. Antagonists would worsen the problem.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic kidney disease who missed dialysis for a week has weakness and a heart rate of 48. Serum potassium is 7.4 mEq per liter. The electrocardiogram shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. Which therapy should be given first?
options: Intravenous regular insulin with dextrose
Nebulized albuterol
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate
Intravenous calcium gluconate
items.explanation: Electrocardiographic changes of hyperkalemia signal imminent arrhythmia, and the first priority is to stabilize the cardiac membrane with intravenous calcium, which acts within minutes but does not lower potassium. Insulin with dextrose and albuterol then shift potassium into cells, and definitive removal requires dialysis in this patient. Oral resins act slowly and cannot be relied on in an emergency. Delaying membrane stabilization while giving shifting agents risks asystole.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has a 6-cm gastric submucosal mass found on endoscopy. A biopsy shows spindle cells that stain positive for KIT. There is no evidence of metastasis. Which operation is most appropriate?
options: Complete resection with negative margins and no formal lymphadenectomy
Total gastrectomy with D2 lymph node dissection to clear the perigastric and celiac nodal basins
Wide margin resection of 5 cm of normal tissue
Radiation therapy alone
items.explanation: A KIT-positive spindle cell gastric tumor is a gastrointestinal stromal tumor, which seldom spreads to lymph nodes. Treatment of a localized lesion is complete surgical resection with negative microscopic margins, avoiding tumor rupture, and no lymphadenectomy is needed. Total gastrectomy with nodal dissection is the operation for adenocarcinoma. Wide margins are unnecessary. These tumors are radioresistant, and imatinib is added for high-risk lesions or unresectable disease.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman recovering from a hip operation on antibiotics develops profuse watery diarrhea. Temperature is 38.5 C, white blood cell count is 22,000 per microliter, and creatinine is 2.1 mg per deciliter. She has no ileus and the abdomen is soft. Stool toxin testing is positive. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Intravenous metronidazole alone
Oral loperamide with probiotic supplements
Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
Urgent total abdominal colectomy
items.explanation: Leukocytosis above 15,000 or creatinine above 1.5 defines severe Clostridioides difficile infection, which is treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Intravenous metronidazole is added only for fulminant disease with ileus or shock, and it is not adequate alone. Antimotility agents risk toxic dilation. Colectomy is reserved for fulminant colitis with shock, perforation, or failure of medical therapy, none of which is present. The inciting antibiotic should be stopped when possible.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man had a transient episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that lasted 30 minutes. Duplex ultrasound shows 80 percent stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Carotid endarterectomy within two weeks with best medical therapy
Medical therapy alone with antiplatelet and statin treatment and repeat imaging in a year
Immediate surgery on the right carotid
Observation until a stroke occurs
items.explanation: Symptomatic internal carotid stenosis above 70 percent confers a high short-term stroke risk, and endarterectomy performed promptly, ideally within two weeks, substantially lowers recurrence when perioperative risk is low. Stenting is an alternative in selected patients. Medical therapy is added but is not enough alone. Weakness in the right arm reflects the left hemisphere, so the right carotid is not the culprit. Waiting for a stroke forfeits the benefit.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy awakens with sudden severe right testicular pain and vomiting. The testis is high-riding and tender, with a horizontal lie and no cremasteric reflex. The pain began 3 hours ago. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Antibiotics for epididymitis and reassessment in two days
Urgent surgical exploration with detorsion and orchiopexy of both testes
Scrotal elevation and anti-inflammatory drugs
Delaying surgery until ultrasound is available if clinical suspicion is high
items.explanation: Acute scrotal pain with a high-riding testis and absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent is testicular torsion, and salvage rates fall sharply after about 6 hours. High clinical suspicion mandates immediate exploration, with orchiopexy on both sides because the bell-clapper anomaly is bilateral. Antibiotics treat epididymitis, which is rare at this age. Imaging should never delay surgery when suspicion is high, and manual detorsion is only a temporary measure.

items.stem: An unconscious 45-year-old man with no identification arrives after a motor vehicle collision with an expanding abdominal hematoma and shock. No family member can be reached. What is the appropriate approach to consent for emergency laparotomy?
options: Delay the operation until a court order or an ethics committee ruling can be obtained
Wait for a family member to arrive to sign the form
Decline surgery because he cannot consent
Proceed under implied consent for the emergency and document the circumstances
items.explanation: In a life-threatening emergency when the patient lacks capacity and no surrogate is available, treatment that a reasonable person would accept proceeds under the emergency exception, or implied consent. The reasoning, the clinicians involved, and attempts to reach family are documented. Seeking a court order or waiting for relatives would cause fatal delay. Refusing care because consent cannot be given abandons the duty to treat. Surrogates are involved as soon as they can be found.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a pelvic fracture with an open-book pattern after a fall from a height. Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg and heart rate is 130. The focused abdominal ultrasound is negative. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Pelvic binder, balanced blood products, and early hemorrhage control by preperitoneal packing or angioembolization
Repeated crystalloid boluses to target a normal blood pressure while awaiting the computed tomography result
Exploratory laparotomy to look for intraperitoneal bleeding first
Delay intervention until computed tomography is completed
items.explanation: Hemodynamic instability with an unstable pelvic ring and a negative abdominal ultrasound points to pelvic bleeding, mostly venous. Management is binder application to reduce volume, balanced transfusion, and hemorrhage control with preperitoneal packing or angioembolization. Crystalloid worsens coagulopathy. Laparotomy is not indicated when the abdomen is not the source and opening it may release tamponade. Taking an unstable patient to scanning before control risks deterioration.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has early satiety and weight loss. Endoscopy shows an antral adenocarcinoma. Staging shows invasion into the muscularis propria with two suspicious perigastric nodes and no distant disease. Which treatment approach is best?
options: Gastrectomy alone with limited D1 nodal sampling
Palliative chemotherapy only without resection because lymph node involvement excludes any curative attempt
Perioperative chemotherapy with gastrectomy and D2 lymphadenectomy
Endoscopic mucosal resection with surveillance
items.explanation: Resectable locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma is treated with perioperative systemic chemotherapy and gastrectomy with adequate margins and D2 lymphadenectomy, which improves survival over surgery alone. Endoscopic resection suits only intramucosal early cancers without nodal risk. Limited node dissection under-stages and leaves disease. Palliative chemotherapy alone is for metastatic or unresectable disease. Staging laparoscopy is used first to exclude peritoneal spread.

items.stem: A 56-year-old woman has rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy shows an adenocarcinoma 7 cm from the anal verge. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging shows a tumor through the muscularis propria with two enlarged mesorectal nodes and a clear circumferential margin. Staging for distant disease is negative. Which treatment sequence is best?
options: Upfront abdominoperineal resection without neoadjuvant therapy
Local transanal excision followed by observation, given the tumor lies within reach of the anus
Adjuvant radiation only after a limited segmental resection
Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by total mesorectal excision
items.explanation: Locally advanced mid rectal cancer with node-positive disease is treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation to downstage the tumor and reduce local recurrence, followed by total mesorectal excision. Abdominoperineal resection is reserved for tumors involving the sphincter complex. Transanal excision is only for small, favorable early lesions without node involvement. Limited segmental resection without mesorectal excision leaves nodal tissue and has high local recurrence.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman is admitted with gallstone pancreatitis. On hospital day 3 she has persistent pain, a heart rate of 100, and no fever. She has pancreatic necrosis on imaging but no sign of infection. She is not tolerating oral intake. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Total parenteral nutrition as the preferred route to rest the pancreas until the pain has resolved
Early enteral nutrition by nasoenteric tube without prophylactic antibiotics
Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics for necrosis
Immediate necrosectomy for sterile necrosis
items.explanation: In severe acute pancreatitis, early enteral feeding maintains the gut barrier and lowers infection and organ failure compared with parenteral nutrition. Prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcomes in sterile necrosis. Debridement is delayed, ideally for several weeks, and is reserved for infected necrosis or specific complications, using minimally invasive step-up approaches. Cholecystectomy for gallstone pancreatitis is timed after recovery, in the same admission for mild disease.

items.stem: Shortly after a peripheral nerve block with bupivacaine for a shoulder procedure, a 58-year-old woman reports perioral numbness and a metallic taste, then has a generalized seizure followed by wide-complex ventricular arrhythmia. Airway and ventilation are supported. Which additional therapy is specifically indicated?
options: Intravenous flumazenil
Intravenous naloxone
Intravenous lipid emulsion
Intravenous atropine alone
items.explanation: Perioral numbness, seizure, and cardiovascular collapse after a regional block indicate local anesthetic systemic toxicity, which is more cardiotoxic with bupivacaine. After airway support and seizure control with a benzodiazepine, intravenous lipid emulsion acts as a sink for the lipophilic drug and is the specific antidote. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and may lower the seizure threshold. Naloxone reverses opioids, and atropine alone does not address ventricular arrhythmia from sodium channel blockade.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has an incidental calcium of 11.4 mg per deciliter and an elevated parathyroid hormone. She has no symptoms. Which additional finding would most strongly support recommending parathyroidectomy?
options: A bone density T-score of minus 2.8 at the forearm
A 24-hour urine calcium that is mildly elevated alone
A vitamin D level in the low normal range
Mild fatigue without other findings
items.explanation: Indications for surgery in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism include age under 50, calcium more than 1 mg per deciliter above normal, osteoporosis by bone density, vertebral fracture, kidney stones or reduced renal function, and high urinary calcium. A T-score at or below minus 2.5 qualifies. Normal vitamin D does not. Vague fatigue is nonspecific, and a modest urine calcium alone does not meet thresholds. Localization imaging guides but does not decide the need for surgery.

items.stem: A severely malnourished 48-year-old man has had a small bowel fistula for six weeks with minimal oral intake. Total parenteral nutrition is started at full caloric goal. Two days later he develops weakness, respiratory muscle fatigue, and confusion. Which laboratory abnormality is the most likely cause?
options: Hypernatremia from the concentrated dextrose load delivered through the central venous catheter
Hypophosphatemia from intracellular shift as insulin rises with feeding
Hypercalcemia from rapid mobilization of bone mineral
Hyperkalemia from release of intracellular stores
items.explanation: Refeeding syndrome follows nutrition in starved patients. Rising insulin drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, and the resulting severe hypophosphatemia impairs ATP production, causing muscle weakness, respiratory failure, and neurologic change. Thiamine deficiency may also manifest. Potassium typically falls rather than rises, and calcium and sodium are not the characteristic disturbances. Prevention is to start slowly at a fraction of the goal, replace electrolytes and thiamine, and monitor daily.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a growing 7-cm mass in the thigh. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a deep heterogeneous lesion. Which step should come next?
options: Immediate marginal excision of the mass through a transverse incision and pathology afterward
Fine-needle aspiration only, then enucleation
Radiation therapy without tissue diagnosis
Core needle biopsy placed along the planned incision line of a future excision
items.explanation: A large deep enlarging soft tissue mass should be considered sarcoma until a tissue diagnosis is made. Core needle biopsy, or an incisional biopsy if necessary, is planned in advance, placed along the axis of the limb so the tract can be removed with definitive resection. Excising the lesion without diagnosis risks positive margins and contaminated planes. Aspiration cytology often cannot determine grade or subtype. Treatment should not start without pathology.

items.stem: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, a 61-year-old man after a hepatectomy develops fever, flank pain, chills, and hypotension. His urine becomes red-brown. What is the most important immediate step?
options: Slow the infusion and give diphenhydramine and acetaminophen, then resume at the usual rate if symptoms settle
Stop the transfusion, keep intravenous access with saline, and verify the unit and patient identification
Continue at the same rate and send a culture of the patient only
Switch to a second unit from a different donor and observe closely for any further fever or rigors
items.explanation: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria during transfusion suggest acute hemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility, usually a clerical error. The transfusion must stop immediately, the line is kept open with saline, identification is rechecked, and the unit and samples are returned to the blood bank. Supportive care includes fluids to maintain urine output. Antihistamines and slowing treat minor reactions. Giving another unit before the cause is established risks a second incompatible exposure.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation not taking anticoagulation has sudden severe pain, pallor, and coolness of the right leg for 4 hours. She cannot move her toes, and sensation is reduced, with arterial Doppler signals absent but venous signals present. What is the best management?
options: Elevation of the leg and observation
Delayed angiography in 48 hours
Immediate systemic anticoagulation and urgent revascularization such as embolectomy
Elective bypass after several weeks of risk factor optimization and a complete cardiac evaluation
items.explanation: A sudden cold limb with motor and sensory loss in a patient with atrial fibrillation is a threatened embolic limb, with a window of only hours before irreversible muscle injury. Anticoagulation prevents propagation, and prompt revascularization by embolectomy or catheter therapy restores flow. Observation or delayed imaging loses viable tissue. Elective bypass applies to chronic ischemia. Reperfusion injury and compartment syndrome should be watched for afterward.

items.stem: A 2-day-old term infant has bilious vomiting and a scaphoid abdomen. The infant is lethargic and mildly dehydrated. An upper gastrointestinal series shows a duodenum that spirals in a corkscrew pattern, with the junction to the right of the midline. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Observation with nasogastric decompression for several days
Elective repair at 6 months of age
Gastrostomy for feeding access
Emergent laparotomy with a Ladd procedure
items.explanation: Bilious emesis in a newborn is a surgical emergency until malrotation with midgut volvulus is excluded. The abnormal junction position and spiraling duodenum confirm it, and delay risks loss of the entire midgut. The Ladd procedure divides the bands, widens the mesentery, and restores bowel position, with appendectomy. Observation allows ischemia to progress. Elective timing is for asymptomatic children, and gastrostomy does not fix the problem.

items.stem: A surgical team studies whether a new mesh reduces hernia recurrence. They compare recurrence rates between two hospitals using different techniques, and the patients at the first hospital are younger and healthier. Which concern most limits the validity of the comparison?
options: Confounding from differences in patient characteristics between the groups
Lack of statistical power from an excessive sample size
Recall bias from retrospective patient interviews
Measurement error from a continuous outcome variable in the recurrence rates
items.explanation: Nonrandom allocation of patients means differences in age and health may explain any difference in recurrence, which is confounding. Randomization or adjustment addresses it. A large sample does not reduce power. Recall bias concerns self-reported exposures, and recurrence is an objective outcome. The outcome here is dichotomous rather than continuous, so measurement of a continuous variable is not the problem.

items.stem: An 80-kg adult has partial and full thickness burns over 40 percent of total body surface area from a house fire two hours ago. Using the Parkland formula, what volume of lactated Ringer solution should be given over the first 8 hours after the burn?
items.explanation: The Parkland formula calls for 4 mL per kilogram per percent burn over 24 hours. For 80 kg and 40 percent that totals 12,800 mL, with half given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury and the rest over the next 16 hours. The total is not the first-period amount, and half of that is not further halved. Rates are then titrated to urine output of about 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a prior hysterectomy has three days of crampy abdominal pain, vomiting, and no flatus. She is hemodynamically stable, the abdomen is distended and mildly tender without peritonitis, and the film shows dilated small bowel with some colonic gas. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Nasogastric decompression, resuscitation, and a water-soluble contrast study
Immediate laparotomy for adhesiolysis
Barium enema to evaluate the colon and exclude a distal large bowel obstruction before any decision
Discharge on a clear liquid diet
items.explanation: A stable patient with a partial adhesive small bowel obstruction and no peritonitis, ischemia, or hernia is managed nonoperatively with decompression and fluids. A water-soluble contrast study is both diagnostic and therapeutic, because arrival of contrast in the colon within 24 hours predicts resolution. Immediate laparotomy is reserved for peritonitis, strangulation, or failure. Barium is avoided because it can cause peritonitis if perforation occurs. Discharge ignores ongoing obstruction.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a painful tear in the posterior midline of the anus with bleeding after bowel movements for 10 weeks. Examination shows a chronic fissure with a sentinel tag and exposed internal sphincter fibers. Fiber, sitz baths, and a topical nitrate have failed. Which treatment is now most appropriate?
options: Fistulotomy of the posterior tract
Excisional hemorrhoidectomy
Lateral internal sphincterotomy
Long-term opioid analgesia for pain
items.explanation: A chronic fissure persists because sphincter hypertonia reduces blood flow to the posterior anoderm. When conservative therapy and topical agents fail, lateral internal sphincterotomy heals most fissures, though it carries a small risk of incontinence. Botulinum injection is an alternative. Fistulotomy treats a fistula, not a fissure. Hemorrhoidectomy addresses a different problem, and opioids worsen constipation and do not treat the cause.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man is hit by a car and has left upper quadrant tenderness. His heart rate is 92 and blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg after one liter of fluid. Computed tomography shows a grade III splenic laceration with a small amount of free fluid and no active contrast extravasation. What is the best management?
options: Immediate splenectomy because any grade III injury requires removal of the organ
Discharge home after one hour of observation
Laparoscopic splenorrhaphy
Nonoperative management with serial examinations and hemoglobin checks in a monitored setting
items.explanation: A hemodynamically stable patient with a blunt splenic injury and no extravasation is managed nonoperatively, which succeeds in most patients and preserves immune function. This requires monitoring, serial hemoglobin, and the ability to operate quickly. Splenectomy is for instability or failure, and angioembolization is added for blush or higher grade injury. Early discharge is unsafe because delayed bleeding can occur. Vaccination is required if the spleen is later removed.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman who has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for rheumatoid arthritis for the past year undergoes a sigmoid colectomy. In the recovery unit she becomes hypotensive at 74/40 mm Hg despite 2 liters of crystalloid and has no bleeding, with sodium 130 and glucose 62. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Begin a norepinephrine infusion and withhold steroids until a cortisol level returns
Give a further 2 liter crystalloid bolus and repeat the lactate in an hour
Give stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone
Return immediately to the operating room for exploration for anastomotic leak
items.explanation: Long-term glucocorticoid use suppresses the adrenal axis, and surgical stress can precipitate adrenal crisis with refractory hypotension, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia. Treatment should not wait for laboratory confirmation, and stress-dose hydrocortisone is given empirically. Vasopressors alone are often ineffective in this setting. More fluid will not fix the underlying deficiency, and reoperation is premature without signs of sepsis or bleeding. Steroid-treated patients should receive perioperative coverage proactively.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man who smokes has a painless, firm, 3-cm left lateral neck mass for six weeks. There is no fever and no sore throat. Examination of the oral cavity and larynx in the office is unremarkable. Which is the best initial diagnostic step?
options: Fine-needle aspiration of the mass with panendoscopy to search for a primary tumor
Open excisional biopsy of the neck mass under general anesthesia before any other test is done
Course of oral antibiotics and reexamination in a month
Total thyroidectomy
items.explanation: A persistent firm lateral neck mass in an adult smoker is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. Fine-needle aspiration gives the diagnosis with minimal risk, and panendoscopy with imaging seeks the primary in the upper aerodigestive tract. Open biopsy risks seeding the neck and complicates later dissection. Antibiotic trials only delay diagnosis. Thyroidectomy is not indicated without evidence the thyroid is the source.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man on postoperative day 6 after pancreaticoduodenectomy has a serum sodium of 119 mEq per liter and a urine osmolality of 540 mOsm per kilogram. He is euvolemic, and urine sodium is 60 mEq per liter. He has mild headache but no seizure. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Rapid correction with hypertonic saline to reach 135 mEq per liter within six hours
Fluid restriction, with hypertonic saline reserved for severe neurologic symptoms
Large volumes of isotonic saline infused until the urine becomes dilute
Free water by mouth to dilute the elevated urine osmolality
items.explanation: Euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine and a high urine sodium indicates inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, common after major surgery. Mild symptoms are treated with fluid restriction, and hypertonic saline is used only for seizures or coma. Overly rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination, so rises should stay below about 8 mEq per liter per day. Isotonic saline can worsen the sodium, and free water deepens dilution.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a 1.2-cm pearly nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasia on the side of his nose. A shave biopsy shows nodular basal cell carcinoma. Which treatment offers the highest cure rate while preserving tissue in this location?
options: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen
Wide excision with 2-cm margins
Topical imiquimod cream
Mohs micrographic surgery
items.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma on the central face is a high-risk site where tissue sparing matters. Mohs micrographic surgery examines the entire margin by frozen section and yields the highest cure rates with maximal tissue preservation. Cryotherapy and topical agents are reserved for superficial low-risk lesions and do not confirm margin clearance. Wide excision is unnecessarily mutilating and may leave a defect that is difficult to reconstruct near the nose.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with prolonged dietary deficiency has a poorly healing surgical wound, perifollicular hemorrhages, and bleeding gums. Which step of collagen synthesis is impaired by his deficiency?
options: Transcription of the collagen gene in fibroblasts
Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen
Cleavage of the terminal propeptides outside the cell by procollagen peptidase after secretion
Cross-linking carried out by an enzyme that needs zinc
items.explanation: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylate procollagen in the endoplasmic reticulum. Without hydroxylation, the triple helix is unstable and collagen is secreted weak, producing scurvy with poor wound healing, bleeding gums, and perifollicular hemorrhage. Gene transcription is not vitamin dependent. Propeptide cleavage and lysyl oxidase cross-linking occur later and use different cofactors. Replacement of the vitamin restores synthesis within days.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation has sudden severe pain, pallor, and paralysis of his left leg. The femoral pulse is present, and the popliteal and distal pulses are absent. The foot is cold and numb. What is the first treatment?
options: Observation with elevation of the limb
Elective angiography in the next several days to plan the eventual revascularization
Major amputation without revascularization
Immediate systemic anticoagulation followed by urgent embolectomy
items.explanation: Sudden onset with absent distal pulses, pallor, and neurologic deficit in a patient with atrial fibrillation indicates acute embolic limb ischemia that is threatened, and the first step is anticoagulation to stop propagation, followed by urgent embolectomy. Waiting loses muscle and nerve within hours. Elevation reduces perfusion. Amputation is for irreversible ischemia, not for a salvageable limb.

items.stem: Two hours after going to bed, a 14-year-old boy wakes with sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomiting. The left testis is high-riding and lies horizontally, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Urinalysis is normal and he has no fever. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate scrotal exploration with detorsion and fixation of both testes
Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and a decision on surgery the next morning
Antibiotics for presumed epididymitis with outpatient follow-up
Manual detorsion at the bedside followed by discharge without surgery
items.explanation: A high-riding horizontal testis with absent cremasteric reflex and acute pain indicates testicular torsion, and salvage depends on operating within about six hours. Clinical suspicion alone justifies exploration, and imaging must not delay it. Both testes are fixed because the anatomic defect is usually bilateral. Antibiotics treat epididymitis, which has a gradual onset and fever. Manual detorsion may be tried but never replaces surgery.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman with advanced pancreatic cancer and capacity declines further chemotherapy and wants comfort-focused care. Her son demands that surgeons operate for a bypass she does not want. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Follow the son's request because family has final authority over a competent patient
Operate since the bypass is low risk
Honor her informed decision and explore her goals with palliative care involvement
Obtain a court order before respecting her refusal
items.explanation: A patient with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse treatment, and surrogates have no authority while she can decide. The surgeon should confirm understanding, discuss alternatives, and involve palliative care to address symptoms. Operating against her wishes is battery despite low risk. A court order is unnecessary because the capacity and refusal are clear and competent.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has a cervical spine fracture after a diving accident. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg, heart rate is 46, and the skin is warm and dry. There is no bleeding on the survey. After a modest fluid bolus he remains hypotensive. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Rapid transfusion of two units of red cells
Pericardial window for suspected tamponade because the pressure is low and the heart rate is slow
Needle decompression of the chest
A vasopressor such as norepinephrine to restore sympathetic tone
items.explanation: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm extremities after a high spinal cord injury is neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic outflow. After limited fluids, vasopressors support perfusion of the injured cord. Blood loss typically causes tachycardia, so transfusion should not be the reflex. Tamponade and tension pneumothorax cause distended neck veins and respiratory signs and tachycardia, which are absent. Hemorrhage must still be excluded before attributing shock to the cord injury alone.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has episodic facial flushing and watery diarrhea. Computed tomography shows a mesenteric mass with spiculated stranding and multiple liver lesions. Biopsy shows a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor from the ileum. Which test best confirms hormone excess?
options: Serum gastrin with a secretin stimulation test to look for a functioning pancreatic tumor
Twenty-four-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid
Fasting serum insulin to glucose ratio
Plasma metanephrines
items.explanation: Flushing and diarrhea with liver metastases from an ileal neuroendocrine tumor define carcinoid syndrome from serotonin that escapes hepatic metabolism. A 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, the serotonin metabolite, confirms the secretion, and somatostatin analogs control symptoms. Gastrin is checked for gastrinoma, insulin for insulinoma, and metanephrines for pheochromocytoma. Preoperative octreotide helps prevent a carcinoid crisis during operation.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has a right colon adenocarcinoma. His father had colon cancer at 45 and an aunt had endometrial cancer. Tumor immunohistochemistry shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression. Which additional result would most favor sporadic methylation rather than Lynch syndrome?
options: Absence of microsatellite instability in the tumor
Loss of MSH2 and MSH6 expression
Presence of a BRAF V600E mutation in the tumor
Presence of numerous adenomas on colonoscopy
items.explanation: Loss of MLH1 and PMS2 can arise from germline mutation or from sporadic promoter hypermethylation. A somatic BRAF V600E mutation or MLH1 promoter methylation points to a sporadic cause, whereas their absence prompts germline testing. Loss of MSH2 and MSH6 indicates a different mismatch repair gene pair. These tumors are microsatellite unstable either way. Numerous adenomas suggest polyposis syndromes rather than Lynch syndrome. Family history here makes testing reasonable.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis from hepatitis C presents with hematemesis. Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg and heart rate 118. After airway assessment and restrictive transfusion, which combination is the most appropriate next therapy?
options: A vasoactive drug such as octreotide, antibiotic prophylaxis, and urgent endoscopic variceal band ligation
A proton pump inhibitor alone with endoscopy the next day
Immediate transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt in every patient before any endoscopy is attempted
Balloon tamponade as first-line therapy
items.explanation: Acute variceal hemorrhage is treated with vasoactive therapy to lower portal pressure, antibiotic prophylaxis to reduce infection and rebleeding, and endoscopy within 12 hours for band ligation. Restrictive transfusion avoids raising portal pressure. Acid suppression alone does not stop variceal bleeding. A shunt is rescue therapy or early in high-risk patients, not universal first therapy. Balloon tamponade is a temporary bridge when endoscopic control fails.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with a mechanical mitral valve takes warfarin and is scheduled for elective inguinal hernia repair in one week. His INR is 3.0. He has no prior stroke or embolic event. Which perioperative plan is most appropriate?
options: Continue warfarin unchanged and operate at an INR of 3.0
Stop warfarin about five days before surgery and bridge with a short-acting parenteral anticoagulant as the INR falls
Stop warfarin five days before surgery and give no bridging anticoagulation
Stop warfarin the evening before surgery and give vitamin K only after the operation
items.explanation: A mechanical mitral valve carries a high thromboembolic risk, so warfarin is held about five days to let the INR fall below 1.5, and bridging is given while the INR is subtherapeutic. Operating at an INR of 3.0 risks bleeding. Stopping without bridging leaves a high-risk valve unprotected. Stopping the night before leaves the INR too high, and vitamin K afterward is irrelevant to surgical bleeding.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm palpable mass in the upper outer left breast. Core biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma, estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative. Imaging shows no suspicious nodes. She wants breast conservation. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Mastectomy with axillary dissection as the only acceptable operation regardless of tumor size
Lumpectomy alone with no radiation
Lumpectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy followed by whole-breast radiation
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy before any operation as standard
items.explanation: A small unifocal invasive cancer with a clinically negative axilla is treated with breast-conserving surgery, sentinel node biopsy, and radiation, which gives survival equal to mastectomy. Omitting radiation increases local recurrence. Axillary dissection is reserved for selected node-positive disease. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is used for larger or triple-negative or HER2-positive tumors. Endocrine therapy follows for her receptor-positive disease.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a serum potassium of 6.9 mEq per liter and peaked T waves with a widened QRS after a crush injury to her leg. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the first medication to administer?
options: Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize the cardiac membrane
Intravenous regular insulin with dextrose to shift potassium into cells
Nebulized albuterol to drive potassium into cells
Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate to remove potassium through the gut
items.explanation: Electrocardiographic changes from severe hyperkalemia call for immediate membrane stabilization with intravenous calcium, which works within minutes but does not lower potassium. Insulin with dextrose and albuterol shift potassium into cells within about 15 to 30 minutes and follow calcium. Binding resins remove potassium slowly over hours and are not emergency therapy. Dialysis is considered when the problem is refractory.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has a 2.2 mm thick melanoma of the back with ulceration confirmed on wide excision biopsy specimen. There is no palpable adenopathy. What is the recommended surgical management?
options: Wide local excision with a 5 mm margin and no nodal evaluation
Wide local excision with a 1 cm margin only
Excision with a 3 cm margin and elective lymph node dissection of the nearest nodal basin
Wide local excision with a 2 cm margin and sentinel lymph node biopsy
items.explanation: Melanomas thicker than 2 mm are excised with a 2 cm margin, and sentinel node biopsy is recommended for intermediate-thickness tumors because nodal status guides adjuvant therapy. A 1 cm margin suits tumors up to 1 mm thick. Narrow margins risk local recurrence. Elective node dissection of clinically negative basins gives no survival benefit over sentinel biopsy and adds morbidity.

items.stem: A 29-year-old man on postoperative day 4 after an emergency appendectomy for perforation has severe incisional pain, skin discoloration with bullae, and crepitus along the lower abdominal wall. He is febrile at 39.4 C with a heart rate of 126 and a blood pressure of 92/54 mm Hg. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Broad-spectrum antibiotics alone with repeat examination in 12 hours
Computed tomography of the abdomen before any operative decision
Resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin, and immediate surgical debridement
Hyperbaric oxygen first, with debridement if no improvement in a day
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, and systemic toxicity indicate necrotizing soft tissue infection, which is a surgical emergency. Survival depends on prompt radical debridement together with antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms, and clindamycin to suppress toxin production. Antibiotics alone are inadequate. Imaging should never delay operation when the diagnosis is clinical. Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive and must not replace debridement.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has a 5.8 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm found on ultrasound. He is asymptomatic, is active, and has acceptable cardiac and pulmonary risk. The anatomy is suitable for either approach. What is the best recommendation?
options: Observation with annual ultrasound only
Elective repair, either endovascular or open, because the diameter exceeds the threshold
Blood pressure control and repeat imaging in three years and a cardiology review before any decision
Emergency repair on the same day
items.explanation: Elective repair is recommended for asymptomatic aneurysms of 5.5 cm or more in men, since annual rupture risk then outweighs perioperative risk. Endovascular repair has lower early mortality and open repair has more durable results, so the choice follows anatomy and fitness. Surveillance suits smaller aneurysms. Emergency repair is for rupture or symptoms, which this patient does not have.

items.stem: A 22-year-old tall man has sudden right chest pain and dyspnea. He has a heart rate of 110, oxygen saturation of 91 percent, and absent breath sounds on the right. Chest radiography shows a 40 percent pneumothorax with no mediastinal shift. What is the best initial treatment?
options: Tube thoracostomy or pigtail catheter drainage with oxygen
Observation without intervention at home
Needle decompression in the second intercostal space as for a tension pneumothorax
Immediate thoracotomy with pleurodesis
items.explanation: A large symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax with hypoxemia needs drainage by small catheter or chest tube. Observation is for small asymptomatic pneumothoraces. Needle decompression treats tension physiology, which causes shift and hypotension, absent here. Surgery with pleurodesis is considered for recurrence or persistent air leak and is not the first step. Smoking cessation lowers recurrence, and reexpansion is confirmed on follow-up radiography.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with pneumonia has progressive hypoxemia on mechanical ventilation. The chest film shows bilateral infiltrates, the ratio of arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen is 110, and echocardiography shows normal left heart function. Which ventilator strategy improves survival?
options: Tidal volume of 12 mL per kilogram to maximize recruitment
Pressure support alone with low positive end-expiratory pressure and early extubation as the main goal
Inspiratory to expiratory ratio kept below one with high peak pressures
Tidal volume of 6 mL per kilogram of predicted body weight with plateau pressure below 30 cm water
items.explanation: Bilateral infiltrates with severe hypoxemia and no cardiac cause define acute respiratory distress syndrome. Lung-protective ventilation with a low tidal volume based on predicted body weight and plateau pressure under 30 cm water reduces mortality by limiting ventilator-induced injury. Large volumes cause volutrauma. Unsupported modes and low pressure fail to keep alveoli open in severe disease. Prone positioning and neuromuscular blockade add benefit for severe cases.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has a three-month history of dysphagia first to solids and then liquids, with a 9 kg weight loss. Endoscopy shows a circumferential mass in the lower esophagus, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. Endoscopic ultrasound shows invasion into the adventitia with three suspicious perigastric nodes. Which treatment sequence is generally preferred?
options: Primary esophagectomy alone without any systemic therapy
Endoscopic mucosal resection with surveillance
Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by esophagectomy
Definitive radiation alone with no operation
items.explanation: A tumor penetrating the adventitia with nodal involvement is locally advanced, and neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by resection improved survival over surgery alone in randomized trials. Endoscopic resection is limited to superficial mucosal cancers. Radiation alone is for patients unfit for surgery. Primary operation without induction therapy gives inferior outcomes in advanced disease. Staging with imaging for distant disease must precede treatment.

items.stem: A 76-year-old man in the intensive care unit after a cardiac operation develops abdominal distention without pain or peritonitis. The film shows a cecum of 12 cm with gas throughout the colon and no transition point. Electrolytes are corrected and no mechanical cause is seen on contrast enema. What is the best next treatment?
options: Intravenous neostigmine with cardiac monitoring
Immediate right hemicolectomy
Oral polyethylene glycol bowel preparation
Observation without any intervention
items.explanation: Massive colonic dilation without a mechanical obstruction is acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, or Ogilvie syndrome. After correcting electrolytes and stopping offending drugs, a cecum near or above 12 cm warrants neostigmine, which resolves most cases but needs monitoring for bradycardia. Surgery is for perforation or ischemia. Oral bowel preparation will not help and may worsen distention. Observation alone risks perforation when the cecum is very large.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman has painless jaundice and weight loss. Computed tomography shows a 3-cm pancreatic head mass abutting the superior mesenteric vein for more than half its circumference, without liver metastases or arterial involvement. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Immediate pancreaticoduodenectomy without further treatment, since the tumor is under 4 cm in diameter
Neoadjuvant systemic therapy and restaging before considering resection
Routine palliative bypass without chemotherapy
Observation with repeat imaging in six months
items.explanation: A pancreatic head tumor with extensive venous contact is borderline resectable, and the risk of positive margins and early systemic relapse favors neoadjuvant therapy, with restaging before an operation aimed at negative margins. Upfront resection is better for clearly resectable tumors. Palliative bypass alone abandons potential cure. Observation for months allows progression of an aggressive cancer. Biliary drainage is used when cholangitis or delay requires it.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops fever, rigidity, and an end-tidal carbon dioxide that climbs rapidly 20 minutes after induction with sevoflurane and succinylcholine. Her temperature is 39.8 C and heart rate is 140. After stopping the volatile agent and hyperventilating with oxygen, which drug should be given next?
options: Acetaminophen given intravenously with surface cooling alone
Neostigmine given intravenously to reverse the neuromuscular blocker, which does not address the hypermetabolic crisis
Calcium gluconate given intravenously to treat the hypercalcemia
Dantrolene given intravenously at a loading dose with repeated boluses as needed
items.explanation: Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, rigidity after succinylcholine, and hyperthermia indicate malignant hyperthermia, caused by uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Dantrolene blocks that release and is the specific antidote. Antipyretics do not act on this mechanism. Neostigmine adds cholinergic stimulation without relieving the hypermetabolism. Calcium would worsen the process, and calcium channel blockers are avoided with dantrolene.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman has bloody nipple discharge from a single duct of the right breast. Mammography and ultrasound show no mass. Cytology is negative. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance and no further evaluation
Bilateral mastectomy to prevent malignancy
Duct excision of the involved duct, since an intraductal papilloma is the most likely cause
Hormone therapy to suppress the discharge
items.explanation: Spontaneous unilateral single-duct bloody discharge is most often caused by an intraductal papilloma, but it can come from malignancy, so negative imaging does not exclude pathology. Duct excision provides diagnosis and treatment. Reassurance risks missing cancer. Mastectomy is excessive. Hormone suppression is used for galactorrhea, which is bilateral, multiduct, milky discharge caused by prolactin. Pathology of the excised duct guides further care.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man in the intensive care unit receives parenteral nutrition after a prolonged ileus following a complicated laparotomy. On the second day of full feeding his phosphate falls from 3.1 to 1.0 mg per dL, and he becomes weak with new tachycardia. He had lost weight for months before admission. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Excess urinary phosphate loss caused by hyperparathyroidism
Insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate during refeeding in a chronically malnourished patient
Impaired intestinal absorption from bile salt deficiency
Binding of phosphate by calcium in the parenteral solution
items.explanation: Refeeding after prolonged starvation raises insulin, which drives glucose, potassium, magnesium, and phosphate into cells and lowers serum levels, sometimes with cardiac and respiratory failure. The prevention is to start nutrition slowly, replace electrolytes, and give thiamine. Hyperparathyroidism and malabsorption are not suggested by this timing. Parenteral solutions are formulated to avoid calcium phosphate precipitation, so that does not explain a sudden fall.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a deep, firm, 9 cm mass in the posterior thigh that has enlarged over six months. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a heterogeneous mass abutting the sciatic nerve. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Excisional biopsy through a transverse incision across the posterior thigh
Marginal enucleation as the final operation
Immediate amputation of the leg
Core needle biopsy placed along the planned incision line
items.explanation: A deep or large soft tissue mass requires tissue diagnosis before treatment, and image-guided core needle biopsy is preferred. The tract is placed so it can be excised with the specimen, because contamination from a transverse incision complicates later limb-sparing resection. Excisional or marginal removal of a probable sarcoma leaves positive margins. Amputation is rarely needed with wide excision and radiation.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman is receiving anticoagulation for a pulmonary embolism. On day 7 of treatment with an intravenous agent, her platelet count falls from 260,000 to 90,000 per microliter, and a new thrombosis appears in her leg. Which medication should replace her current therapy?
options: A direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban, after stopping the current agent
Warfarin started immediately at full dose
Platelet transfusion to correct the thrombocytopenia
Increased dose of the current anticoagulant to treat the new clot and keep the infusion running
items.explanation: A platelet fall of more than half between days 5 and 10 with new thrombosis suggests an immune-mediated, prothrombotic drug thrombocytopenia from the anticoagulant, which requires stopping the offending agent and starting a different anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux. Warfarin alone can cause venous limb gangrene early. Platelet transfusion feeds thrombosis. Increasing the dose of the current drug worsens the immune process.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man with diabetes has a nonhealing foot ulcer, rest pain, and absent pedal pulses. The ankle-brachial index is 0.35. Angiography shows long segment occlusion of the superficial femoral and tibial arteries, and he has adequate saphenous vein. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Local wound care and antibiotics without revascularization
Revascularization, with bypass using vein when anatomy is unsuitable for endovascular treatment
Supervised exercise therapy as the sole treatment
Lumbar sympathectomy as primary treatment
items.explanation: Rest pain and tissue loss define chronic limb-threatening ischemia, where healing requires restoration of flow. Long occlusions with good vein often favor bypass, while shorter lesions may be treated endovascularly. Wound care cannot heal an ischemic ulcer. Exercise therapy is for claudication. Sympathectomy rarely improves limb salvage. Smoking cessation, statins, and antiplatelet therapy are given to every patient.

items.stem: A 3-week-old boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed and is hungry afterward. A palpable olive-shaped mass is felt in the epigastrium. Blood tests show hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with a chloride of 88 mEq per liter. What is the next step?
options: Immediate pyloromyotomy before any resuscitation
Trial of acid suppression for several weeks
Correct fluid and electrolyte abnormalities before pyloromyotomy
Upper gastrointestinal series for malrotation first, before any other step
items.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis presents with projectile nonbilious vomiting and a palpable olive, and the metabolic disturbance is corrected with saline and potassium before surgery, because anesthesia in an alkalotic infant risks apnea. Pyloromyotomy is then curative. Acid suppression does not treat the obstruction. Imaging for malrotation applies to bilious vomiting, and ultrasound confirms stenosis when the mass is unclear.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man is struck by a car and arrives with a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg, a heart rate of 134, and a positive focused ultrasound examination showing free fluid in the right upper quadrant. He responds only transiently to blood. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate laparotomy for hemorrhage control
Abdominal computed tomography with intravenous contrast
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage in the emergency department
Angioembolization of the liver before any operation
items.explanation: A hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient with a positive ultrasound examination has intraperitoneal hemorrhage until proven otherwise and needs immediate laparotomy. Computed tomography requires stability and wastes time. Peritoneal lavage is no longer needed when ultrasound already shows fluid. Angioembolization suits stable patients with contrast blush on imaging. Resuscitation with balanced blood products continues in parallel.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has episodic epigastric pain and a fasting gastrin of 1,400 pg per mL with gastric pH of 1.5. She has recurrent duodenal and jejunal ulcers. Computed tomography does not show a pancreatic mass. Which additional condition should be assessed?
options: Pheochromocytoma, because of possible multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2
Medullary thyroid carcinoma, because of calcitonin elevation
Carcinoid syndrome, because of serotonin overproduction
Primary hyperparathyroidism, because of possible multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
items.explanation: A markedly raised gastrin with low gastric pH and refractory ulcers indicates gastrinoma, and about a quarter of cases occur with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, which includes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors. Treating hypercalcemia first lowers gastrin. Pheochromocytoma and medullary thyroid cancer belong to the type 2 syndromes. Carcinoid syndrome causes flushing and diarrhea rather than ulcers.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man has a palpable mass 6 cm from the anal verge. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging shows a tumor invading through the muscularis propria with threatened mesorectal fascia and four enlarged mesorectal nodes. No distant disease is found. What is the best initial approach?
options: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation or total neoadjuvant therapy before total mesorectal excision
Upfront low anterior resection followed by adjuvant therapy
Transanal local excision with pathologic review
Palliative chemotherapy alone
items.explanation: A locally advanced rectal cancer with a threatened circumferential margin and nodal disease benefits from neoadjuvant treatment, which downstages the tumor and lowers local recurrence before total mesorectal excision. Upfront surgery risks a positive margin. Local excision is limited to small, early, favorable tumors. Palliative chemotherapy alone is wrong because the disease is localized and curable.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain, fever, jaundice, and confusion with a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with stones. Intravenous antibiotics and fluids are started. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate open cholecystectomy with common duct exploration
Urgent biliary decompression by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy within the next admission
Magnetic resonance cholangiography and a delay until she improves before any procedure
items.explanation: Fever, jaundice, hypotension, and confusion constitute Reynolds pentad of severe ascending cholangitis, where mortality falls with early decompression, ideally by endoscopic drainage. Open common duct exploration in a septic patient carries high mortality. Cholecystectomy is deferred until the infection resolves. Additional imaging delays drainage. Percutaneous transhepatic drainage is the alternative if endoscopic access fails. Source control is the priority.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a body mass index of 36, and obstructive sleep apnea on home positive airway pressure is scheduled for colectomy. Which perioperative step most reduces his risk of postoperative respiratory failure?
options: Withhold his positive airway pressure device until he is fully awake on the ward
Give long-acting benzodiazepines the night before surgery to reduce anxiety
Use his positive airway pressure device after extubation and limit opioid dosing with multimodal analgesia
Plan routine postoperative intubation and ventilation for the first full day
items.explanation: Patients with sleep apnea are prone to airway collapse and opioid-related respiratory depression, so continuing their pressure device and sparing opioids with regional or nonopioid analgesia lowers pulmonary complications. Withholding the device removes protection during the riskiest period. Sedatives increase airway collapse. Routine prolonged ventilation is unnecessary and adds pneumonia and delirium risk without proven benefit.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heart rate of 118, and a diffusely enlarged thyroid with a bruit. Radioactive iodine uptake is diffusely increased at 60 percent. She is not pregnant and has no eye disease. Which treatment is most appropriate for definitive control?
options: Levothyroxine given at a suppressive dose
Observation until the thyrotoxicosis resolves spontaneously as the disease burns out
Immediate total thyroidectomy without medical preparation
Radioactive iodine ablation after beta-blocker and thionamide preparation
items.explanation: Diffuse high uptake and a bruit indicate Graves disease, and definitive options are radioactive iodine, surgery, or long-term thionamides. Beta-blockers control symptoms, and thionamides render the patient euthyroid. Levothyroxine worsens thyrotoxicosis. Graves disease rarely remits spontaneously. Operating while thyrotoxic risks thyroid storm. Iodine is avoided in pregnancy, and active ophthalmopathy favors surgery or steroid cover.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a 5 cm gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the stomach that expresses KIT, confirmed by biopsy. There is no metastasis, and the tumor is resectable. What is the surgical principle for this tumor?
options: Wide resection with extensive regional lymph node dissection
Enucleation with positive margins followed by observation
Complete resection with negative margins without routine lymphadenectomy, preserving the pseudocapsule
Total gastrectomy with splenectomy as routine treatment
items.explanation: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors seldom spread to lymph nodes, so resection aims for negative margins, with wedge or segmental resection and an intact pseudocapsule to avoid rupture, which carries high recurrence. Lymphadenectomy and total gastrectomy add morbidity without benefit. Positive margins and observation risk local recurrence. Imatinib is considered adjuvantly according to risk features such as size and mitotic rate.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man undergoing a hernia repair received a first dose of cefazolin. Within five minutes he develops urticaria, wheezing, a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg, and facial swelling. After stopping the drug and securing the airway, which is the first-line medication?
options: Intramuscular epinephrine given immediately and repeated if symptoms persist
Intravenous diphenhydramine as the primary treatment
Intravenous methylprednisolone as the primary treatment to blunt the immune-mediated reaction
Nebulized albuterol alone for the bronchospasm
items.explanation: Hypotension, bronchospasm, and angioedema after an antibiotic indicate anaphylaxis, whose first-line treatment is epinephrine, given early to reverse vasodilation and bronchospasm. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts that work too slowly to treat shock and may only blunt late reactions. Albuterol treats wheezing alone and does not restore perfusion. Fluids and airway support accompany epinephrine, and delay in giving it is linked to worse outcomes.

items.stem: A 5-year-old boy has a nontender abdominal mass that crosses the midline and wraps around the aorta. He has periorbital ecchymoses and elevated urine catecholamine metabolites. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Wilms tumor
Neuroblastoma
Hepatoblastoma
Burkitt lymphoma
items.explanation: Neuroblastoma arises from sympathetic tissue, often in the adrenal gland, crossing the midline and encasing vessels, with raised urinary catecholamine metabolites and periorbital ecchymoses from orbital metastases.
